question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.
essay:
Hong Kong should tighten its rules on subdivided units (SDUs), but the tightening should be about security of tenure and a light limit on rent increases, not a hard cap on rent levels. 

My first view was that SDU tenants are poor, landlords have the power, and so rents should be capped harder. The first part is true. SDUs hold about 110,000 households, and tenants pay a premium of 15 to 25 percent per square foot compared with ordinary flats, because the space is priced at its most desperate margin [D1p1]. Most tenants are new arrivals or people waiting for public housing, so the SDU is a last option, not a choice [D1p2]. And the current rules are not enough. Rent burden for SDU households rose from 31 to 34 percent of income [D2p2]. The 2021 ordinance capped increases inside a tenancy but not the initial rent [D1p3].

The second part of my first view, that a stronger cap is the fix, did not hold up. A working paper separates hard caps on rent levels from caps on increases within a tenancy. Hard caps consistently shrink supply, while the second kind has small or null effects, and Hong Kong's 2021 law is the second kind [D6p2]. The numbers fit: the stock of SDUs grew from 100,800 in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 [D2p1]. The harm of shrinking supply falls on the same poor households the cap is meant to help [D6p3]. Berlin gives a rough warning. After its 2020 cap, listings fell and owners moved flats to uncontrolled segments [D7p1], and the tenants protected were those already inside while the cost went to those outside [D7p3].

The landlords say they will leave if returns fall [D5p2]. I take this seriously but not at face value. Their own data is weak: the cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate, and they admit they have no data on actual margins [D5p3]. Mr Chan, a tenant, has seen two units on his floor emptied [D3p2], so the fear is not invented, but the stock figures show no mass exit under the milder control.

What do tenants actually need? In a survey of 440 households, the main problem named was queue length and insecurity of tenure, not the rent level, and 61 percent would accept a small rent rise for three years of security [D11p1]. Mr Chan's landlord ended an earlier tenancy with two weeks notice after he asked for a window repair [D3p1].

This is also why enforcement matters. Inspections cover under 6 percent of SDU stock each year [D10p1]. Enforcement depends on complaints, but the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement and the newest arrivals [D10p2]. Mrs Wong has lived in her SDU for nine years without ever receiving a written agreement, and she says the 2021 ordinance changed nothing for her [D4p1]. Her case shows how my idea could fail: protection that depends on paperwork misses the people who most need it. So the law should presume a tenancy after a set time, even with no paper, and ban eviction as punishment for complaints.

There is a serious objection. The NGO report says rent caps treat a price symptom of a quantity problem, and that enforcement staff spent policing rents are not spent on safety inspections, where the harm is documented [D11p2]. I accept part of this. The root problem is the queue, which is about five and a half years [D1p2], and a policy on SDUs cannot fix that alone. Also, a heavy initial-rent register would be expensive, since one estimate is 40 to 60 staff-years [D10p1]. So I would keep any band on initial rents light, as the report itself supports [D11p3], and put the main effort into tenure, which tenants can enforce themselves through a tribunal and which needs fewer inspectors.

I should be honest about two limits. First, the archive does not tell me how many tenants have no written agreement. Second, an internal minute admits that nobody found an enforcement design that protects the newest arrivals first rather than last [D10p3]. Presuming a tenancy helps people who stay, but not someone who has just arrived, and a band on initial rents could even make landlords less willing to take newcomers, as the Berlin case hints [D7p3].

So my position is yes, tighten, but carefully. Cap increases more firmly, protect tenants from retaliation, presume a tenancy without paper, keep any initial-rent band light, and treat the waiting list as the real long-term fix.

turns.text: I think Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units. Reasons: (1) tenants in tiny subdivided flats are poor and have little bargaining power, so landlords can raise rent easily; (2) housing is a basic need and rents should not eat most of a poor family's income; (3) controls can come with minimum safety standards so living conditions improve.
Earlier you said controls can come with minimum safety standards — what leads you from rent control to landlords actually meeting those standards?

Honestly I am not sure rent control alone makes landlords meet standards. Maybe it needs inspections too. Can you show me sources about subdivided units, rents and rent control in Hong Kong so I can test this?

You've said two things there: rent control alone may not make landlords meet standards, and inspections might be the missing piece. Before I point you anywhere, what would a source need to show for you — evidence that rent control changed landlord behaviour, a counter-view, or a first-hand account from a subdivided unit tenant?
I want all three if possible, but first evidence on whether rent control changed landlord behaviour or rents in Hong Kong, and a counter-view that argues against it.

Tenant source: evidence the current control is too weak or that tenants fear eviction if they complain. Enforcement source: it should support my claim that a tighter increase-cap only works if someone actually checks landlords follow it.

This changes my view a lot. D11p1 says tenants care more about tenure security and queue length than rent level, and D3p1 shows eviction after asking for a repair. D10p1 says inspections cover under 6 percent of stock, and D10p2 says the people who most need protection can't complain. So a rent-cap tightening alone would mostly not reach the worst cases. I now think: tighten, but make the tightening about security of tenure (protection from retaliation) plus a light cap on increases, not a lower rent level. A possible objection from D11p2 is that enforcement money should go to safety inspection instead of policing rent. I answer: security of tenure is cheap to enforce through the courts and it makes complaints possible, so it helps both goals. Can you give me structure options for the essay?

Three tracks, pick one and say why:

1. **Claim → evidence → objection → reply** — good if your main move is defending the tenure-security-plus-light-cap position against D11p2.
2. **Problem → cause → response** — good if you want the 31-to-34 percent burden and the 6 percent inspection figure to set up why the current control fails.
3. **Compare and contrast** — good if you want to weigh the increase-cap-only view against your revised view, using D2p1/D6p2 on one side and D6p1/D6p3/D5p2 on the other.

Which one fits what you most want to say, and why?
I pick option 1, claim, evidence, objection, reply, because my position changed into a specific claim and the strongest objection (D11p2 and the landlord exit threat in D5p2) needs a direct answer.

Good — you've named the claim and the objection it has to survive. One thing to settle before you draft: is D5p2's landlord-exit threat part of the *same* objection as D11p2, or a second objection you answer separately? Your reply about cheap court enforcement speaks to D11p2's funding trade-off, but does it also answer landlords leaving?

Good question. I think they are two objections. Landlord exit I answer with D2p1 and D6p2 (moderate second-generation control did not shrink stock) and D5p3 (their numbers are self-reported with a 34 percent response rate). The funding trade-off I answer with the court route. But D3p2 says Mr Chan has seen units emptied, so the exit fear is not made up. Can I look at the sources about newly arrived tenants and tenants with no written agreement, to see if my tenure idea actually reaches them?

You've said D3p2 keeps the exit fear alive, and you want to check whether your tenure idea reaches newly arrived tenants and those without written agreements. What would a source on those two groups need to show for you — evidence that they're covered by your idea, or a counter-view that they're not?
A counter-view, honestly: I want it to show whether those groups are NOT covered, because that is where my idea could fail. Any numbers on how many tenants have no written agreement would help.

D4p1 is a problem for my idea: Mrs Wong has no written agreement and says the 2021 ordinance changed nothing for her, so a tenure rule only works if it covers people without paperwork. D1p3 says the 2021 law did not cap initial rent, which is a gap newcomers fall into (D1p2 says SDU tenants are mostly new arrivals). So I refine again: the tenure protection must apply by law even with no written agreement (a tenancy is presumed after a set time), and a light band on initial rents should go with it, as D11p3 says. D4p2 says hard cap, but D4p3 shows her own stairwell lost two flats, so her belief that landlords cannot exit is contradicted by her own account. I keep my position, now narrower.

You've refined the claim so tenure protection applies without written agreements and added a light band on initial rents, and you're using D4p3 against D4p2's hard-cap view. What would you want to check next — whether D1 or D11 gives any figure on how many tenants lack written agreements, or how your reply handles D4p1's point that the 2021 ordinance changed nothing for her?

I checked D1 and D11: neither gives a figure for how many tenants lack written agreements, so I will say that is a gap in the evidence. On D4p1, my reply is that the ordinance failed her because it relied on a written tenancy and on her complaining, which is what D10p2 predicts. So presuming a tenancy by law fixes the exact failure she describes.
You've said what D1, D11, D4p1 and D10p2 do for you — so what would a new source need to show that none of those four already show, and which of your claims would it be backing?

One more weakness I should admit: D10p3 says the subcommittee could not find any enforcement design that protects the newest arrivals first. My answer is only partial: tenure by presumption helps people who stay, but not someone who just arrived. Is there anything left in the archive on this that I have not seen?

But Berlin was a very different market (1.5 million flats, ordinary housing) so I should say it is only a loose comparison. Document D11, the NGO report, argues that rent caps treat the price symptom of a quantity problem, and that enforcement capacity spent policing rents is capacity not spent on safety inspection — where the harm is documented and immediate.

How do you answer this?

I partly agree with D11p2: the queue is the root problem and safety inspection matters. But tenure security does not need many inspectors, because it is enforced by tenants going to a tribunal, so it does not take much from inspection staff. And I would not spend the 40 to 60 staff-years in D10p1 on a rent register; I would drop the heavy initial-rent band and keep it light. So I accept the point about priorities and narrow my claim.
You've said you partly agree with D11p2 and would drop the heavy band to keep inspection capacity free. What in D10p1 or D11p2 tells you how much enforcement capacity a light band would still need?
